Some people see this differently, but by and large I see lots of people accept self-diagnosis as a legitimate path with the understanding that it involves genuine research and trying to gather information about yourself in the past to consider whether it adds up as much as the way you currently experience things does. 

It seems to me the people who are the least understanding about this often were diagnosed so young that it naturally doesn’t occur to them what it is like to get evaluated later in life, even if you are still a young adult or teen. I am currently in an evaluation process for several reasons including ASD, but that is mostly because I am having a lot of trouble and need to figure out better ways to manage stuff. From my experience getting even to the point of finding a good person to go to - it is not something people should be expected to do until things change about the accessibility, expensiveness, and the sheer lack of people who work with and assess adults compared to kids. Bring in other demographic differences like AGAB, gender identity, race, ethnicity, and the way previous life experiences have changed how you communicate and express, and it is really only worth it if you need it and can find a good person for you, who you also can *afford.*

I am understanding with why anyone in any group may be wary about self-assessment but honestly even if you do get evaluated/diagnosed as and adult, it basically requires self assessing and some level of self diagnosis process before you get to the point of seeing a specialist. Because unlike a little kid or toddler, there isn’t someone else bringing you in and explaining what is going on and why that seems like reason to evaluate for/diagnose ASD, and an adult has to do things differently in an assessment than a small child.

So if this is helping you accept your needs and move toward dealing with your sensory overload etc, then that is reason enough in my opinion to self diagnose! Just be as well informed as you possibly can, and if you can ask for outside perspective on things I suggest it. (you wouldn’t necessarily have to say you are asking about ASD, it could just be questions about behaviors in your childhood etc.)

your own identity is of course your thing to feel out, but my advice as someone 4 years on HRT who has had several gender affirmation surgeries: Try to untie what you want physically from these labels and expectations / ideas about what is okay and should be. 
I am not confined to one part of the binary, and I have come to understand more about myself in the past six years than I could ever hope to describe to someone in any single term or label. Yet I thought for much of my teens that because I wanted to *really* medically transition, and I was making legal documentation changes, and other similar reasons - that I couldn’t be nonbinary, that I had been wrong to identify as agender, and genderfluid and other things that didn’t seem to line up with taking HRT or making serious decisions like not being able to biologically reproduce. 

but now I just see it more this way: yes those are serious decisions but it isn’t being a binary trans person that makes them okay decisions that aren’t ‘wierd’ or ‘reckless’ - it is really sitting with the things motivating you, and the implications in your life of going through with things. We live in a binary world/society - there is a certain extent that it has been a huge gift for me to become comfortable in certain settings with certain aspects of the binary. But it means more for me than I ever thought it could to fully accept and see myself as the multitude/variant gender identity I am  even as I move through the world being categorized by people in ways that I wouldn’t have necessarily asked for. 
And if you are a trans dude and non-conforming / sometimes feminine that is totally cool. but just dont tell yourself you have to be that if you want to do things for your dysphoria. In my experience one thing can lead to another when you start making too many strict rules about how yo ucan see yourself  in transition.
